clue.text: My godson seems almost wild

indicators.note: wild says the combined letters run riot and are rearranged
almost means the word seems is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: the word seems, which loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that their godson seems almost out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like the possessive opening the sentence, but it is the exclamation of surprise. 'almost' trims SEEMS to SEEM, and 'wild' jumbles that with GODSON.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise, so the interjection 'My!' means the same as this old-fashioned phrase.

clue.text: Forbidding finally crossing border

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of the next word is used

parts.note: last letter of the word
a rim is an edge or border

explanation.surface: Something ominous happens as someone finally steps over a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forbidding' reads as a verb about prohibition, but here it is the adjective meaning stern and threatening.
explanation.definitionFit: A forbidding expression or landscape is stern, harsh and unwelcoming, which is what grim describes.

clue.text: Quick to notice biblical book lacks first page?

indicators.note: lacks first means the book's name goes without its first letter

parts.note: Job is a book of the Old Testament
a page is a boy servant

explanation.surface: A sharp-eyed reader spots a Bible missing its opening page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first page' looks like one phrase, but it splits: 'lacks first' cuts the J from JOB, and 'page' is a junior servant, as in a pageboy.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone observant is alert and perceptive, quick to notice details others miss.

clue.text: Regularly infer editor's requirements

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: second and fourth letters
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor
the apostrophe S taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer is told to read between the lines to work out what the editor wants.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's is not just grammar; it supplies the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Needs as a plural noun are the things required, so the word is a direct synonym of requirements.

clue.text: Start keeping worthless dog tied up

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a seed is the start or origin of something
a cur is a mongrel or worthless dog

explanation.surface: Someone begins by keeping a useless mutt on a leash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start' looks like an instruction but is a noun: a seed is the beginning from which something grows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something secured has been fastened firmly, as a boat or parcel tied up with rope is made fast.

clue.text: Gains a thorough knowledge of 1,000 plants

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
asters are daisy-like garden flowers

explanation.surface: A gardener becomes expert in a thousand different plants.
explanation.walkthrough: The number is a Roman numeral, and 'plants' means one particular flower family rather than plants in general.
explanation.definitionFit: To master a subject is to learn it completely and acquire full command of it, a verb in the same third person.

clue.text: State again wanting carbon cut

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so a letter is missing from the word

parts.note: to recap is to restate the main points
C is the chemical symbol for carbon, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A report demands that carbon emissions be reduced again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carbon cut' looks like an environmental slogan, but 'cut' is the definition and carbon is just its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: To reap is to harvest grain by mowing it down with a scythe or sickle, so it means to cut.

clue.text: Muslim leader always embraces this writer

indicators.note: to embrace is to hug, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever
the setter referring to themself

explanation.surface: A writer boasts that an Islamic ruler always welcomes them warmly.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a less common spelling of emir. 'This writer' is the setter, giving ME.
explanation.definitionFit: An emeer or emir is a ruler or commander in Muslim countries, a title used for princes and governors.

clue.text: Do assemble below gap in the mountains

indicators.note: in a down clue below means placed underneath, so the piece named first comes second in the grid

parts.note: a pass is a route through a mountain range
to muster is to gather troops together

explanation.surface: An instruction to gather below a mountain col.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'below' means the second piece sits under the first. 'Do' is the definition, in the sense 'that will do'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that will do is adequate; to pass muster is to be judged acceptable or good enough after inspection.

clue.text: Think about prisoners on island, ruddy upset

parts.note: cons are convicts
I is the abbreviation for island

indicators.note: to upset is to tip over, and in a down clue that turns the word upside down

parts.note: ruddy means reddish

explanation.surface: Someone muses on convicts on an island who are bloody annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy' reads as the mild British swear word, but it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: To consider is to ponder or reflect upon something, a plain synonym of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Problem in the US simply rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run backwards
in signals that the letters are found inside the words that follow

parts.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A difficulty in America is simply dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across 'thE US SImply' and must be read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is a matter of dispute or a difficulty, as in 'that is the issue', so it means a problem.

clue.text: Doctor cures most clients

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or falsify, so the letters are altered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A GP successfully treats the majority of patients.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like the subject of the sentence but is a verb meaning tamper with.
explanation.definitionFit: Clients and customers are both people who buy goods or services from a business; they are synonyms.

clue.text: Keep quiet about what Novak Djokovic might do

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
re means concerning or about
a tennis player serves

explanation.surface: Someone urges silence on the subject of a tennis star's conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep quiet' reads as one phrase meaning hush, but 'Keep' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To preserve something is to maintain it or retain it unchanged, a direct synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Initially some cows and sheep get lost

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letters are taken

parts.note: first letters of each word
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A farmer finds a few cattle and sheep have wandered off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get lost' looks like it describes straying livestock; it is the rude instruction to go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Scram is an informal command to leave at once, the same brusque dismissal as telling someone to get lost.

clue.text: RAF accepts new rocket?

indicators.note: something new has been remade, so the letters take a fresh form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Royal Air Force takes delivery of a new missile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accepts' looks like a verb linking the RAF to the rocket; it is just more letters to rearrange. The question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocket is one example of a vehicle built to travel beyond the atmosphere, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Padre is bizarrely commended

indicators.note: bizarrely means in a strange way, so the letters are arranged oddly

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An army chaplain is oddly singled out for an award.
explanation.walkthrough: A padre is a military chaplain; here he only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To commend someone is to speak well of them publicly, the same as praising them; both are past forms.

clue.text: Most wee from cat smells around Charlie's shed

indicators.note: around says the remaining letters are moved about into a new order
the 's means has, and has shed says the letter for Charlie is dropped from cat smells

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone notices cat urine smells around a garden shed belonging to Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wee' and 'shed' play on cat pee and a garden hut. 'shed' drops the C from CAT SMELLS, leaving ATSMELLS, and 'around' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Wee is Scottish and informal for small, so the superlative most wee means the smallest.

clue.text: Small oars scratching top of picnic hampers

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small

indicators.note: scratching means withdrawing or crossing out, and top points to the first letter

parts.note: paddles are short oars
first letter of the word, which is removed

explanation.surface: Little oars scrape the lid of a wicker picnic basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hampers' looks like the baskets but is a verb, meaning burdens.
explanation.definitionFit: To saddle someone with a task is to burden them with it, which hinders or hampers them.

clue.text: Constable maybe produced this bag and small cloak

parts.note: to bag is to land or secure, as a fish or prize
S is the abbreviation for small
a cape is a sleeveless cloak

explanation.surface: A policeman apparently made up a bag and short cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable' suggests a police officer, but it is John Constable, the English painter of rural scenes.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable was famous for painting rural scenery such as The Hay Wain, so a picture of countryside is what he produced.

clue.text: Too much silver found in church residence

indicators.note: found in means located inside, so these pieces go within another

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
OTT is over the top
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: An excessive quantity of silver is discovered in a vicarage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church residence' reads as a parsonage, but the two words split: church is the container, residence the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cottage is a small house, especially in the country, so it is a kind of residence.

clue.text: European cross with dodgy plan I describe

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or dubious, so the letters are not to be trusted in their order

parts.note: an X is a cross
taken as written

explanation.surface: An angry continental is outlining a suspect scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry, but it is the letter X.
explanation.definitionFit: To explain something is to set it out in words clearly, which is to describe or account for it.

clue.text: Unusual row after second tango

indicators.note: after means coming behind, so the piece named first goes at the end of the answer

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
Tango is T in the NATO alphabet
a range is a row or line, as of mountains

explanation.surface: An odd quarrel erupts during a second dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests an argument; it is a line of things. 'After' places it behind the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Strange and unusual both describe something out of the ordinary, odd or unfamiliar.

clue.text: Besotted with German after last of tweets on X

indicators.note: the last of something is its end, so the final letter is taken

parts.note: final letter
mit is German for with
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: Someone is infatuated after reading posts on the social network X.
explanation.walkthrough: X looks like the social media platform, but it is the Roman numeral. In a down clue 'on' means placed after.
explanation.definitionFit: Being smitten is being struck with love or infatuation, the same as being besotted with someone.

clue.text: Mammal moved nearer lake

parts.note: came means approached
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: An animal edges closer to the water.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is general; the camel is one example of a mammal.
explanation.definitionFit: A camel is a large humped mammal of the desert, so it is one instance of the broad class named.

clue.text: Maiden begs for veils

parts.note: M is maiden, an over with no runs in cricket scoring
to beg is to ask

explanation.surface: A young woman pleads for face coverings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Veils' reads as nouns but is a verb meaning conceals. A maiden over in cricket is one in which no runs are scored.
explanation.definitionFit: To mask something is to hide or disguise it, just as to veil it is to cover and conceal it.

clue.text: Victorian grew flower

parts.note: prim, stiffly proper, as Victorian manners were
rose means increased or went up

explanation.surface: A nineteenth-century gardener cultivated a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victorian' looks like a historical person but is an adjective for strait-laced propriety.
explanation.definitionFit: The primrose is a pale yellow wild spring bloom, one example of a flower.

clue.text: Breed fish, we're told

indicators.note: what we are told is heard rather than read, so sound matters

parts.note: rays are flat sea fish

explanation.surface: A fish farmer is instructed to rear stock.
explanation.walkthrough: The flat fish and the verb sound the same but are spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise animals is to rear or breed them, as a farmer raises cattle or pigs.

clue.text: Kinky inclination

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a natural leaning or talent

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like a suggestive pairing, but one is an adjective and the other a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A bent wire is kinked rather than straight, and a bent for music is a natural inclination or aptitude.

clue.text: Someone who helps animal is hesitant? Not half!

parts.note: an ass is an animal, a donkey

indicators.note: not half means half the letters of hesitant are taken away, the first four

parts.note: the word hesitant, which keeps only its second half

explanation.surface: A helper asks whether an animal is reluctant, and gets an emphatic reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' reads as British slang for 'very much so', but here it removes HESI, the first half of HESITANT, leaving TANT.
explanation.definitionFit: An assistant is a person employed or acting to help someone else with their work.

clue.text: Silly bats ignoring spades

indicators.note: to ignore is to leave out, so a letter is left out

parts.note: bats is slang for crazy
S is the abbreviation for spades in card games, the letter removed

explanation.surface: Foolish cricket bats are left without garden spades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the flying mammals or cricket bats but is slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means pointless and foolish, lacking sense, so it is a synonym of silly.

clue.text: First-rate student welcomes exam

indicators.note: to welcome is to take inside, so the letters sit within the words before

parts.note: letters spanning the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: A top pupil greets an examination with pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First-rate' looks like a description of the student, but it is part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: A test is an exam, an assessment of knowledge or ability; the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Where riders might compete, no matter what

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: horse riders compete within a sporting fixture

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is the phrase taken literally, as in equestrian eventing; the second is its everyday idiomatic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means regardless of circumstances or whatever happens, so it matches the phrase of insistence.
